items.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: And now, at this point, two people which is Nancy Wilson and Joe Williams, and Henry Johnson, I work with

ctx.x: Although once a year I go and make sure — a check-up and all that. But it worked out fine for me. I was very fortunate. I had one of the top specialists in that field at the time. And then I decided this is too much pressure, all these people and I sort of cut back on it, and finally down to maybe three or four people. And now, at this point, two people which is Nancy Wilson and Joe Williams, and Henry Johnson, I work with because he’s with Joe and anything I can do to work with him is fine, and we’re very close.…

That’s great. When you first started working with Joe then, he had come out of that period where he’d had the hit with the Basie band. Was there a conscious decision with you guys at that point where you said okay, I did the big band thing, now I’m ready for a solo career, or did you find a group to play with him or was he kind of freelancing with different bands?

items.title: Nancy Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995
items.q: By the time I went with John, he had Ramsey Lewis, Gene Harris, The Three Sounds, he had Cannonball, I mean he had so many wonderful artists that he nurtured

ctx.x: No. No I think we were all pretty much on a — at that time — we’re talking about time that made the difference, as opposed to where you were. Maybe if you were in, if I’d have been in Kansas City I might have sung more blues or R&B. But what I heard as a child, was Little Jimmy Scott, Nat Cole, Bull Moose Jackson, Laverne Baker, Ruth Brown, Dinah. Basically male influences first. Louis Jordan and the Tympani Five. My father was the one who bought records. Consequently what I heard were male influences. I found…

did such a good job for George, that just opened the door. By the time I went with John, he had Ramsey Lewis, Gene Harris, The Three Sounds, he had Cannonball, I mean he had so many wonderful artists that he nurtured and made sure that they took care of the business and did wonderful things for them. So the object of my strategy was, if I’m going to do this, the only person who I would trust to help and be there for me would be John Levy.
What a rare commodity — to have a musician, a fine musician, who would step into that role. “I want to be with him.”

items.title: Nancy Wilson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Generally, I – we’ d just – we’d sit down, me, John, Dave, sit at my house, go over the music, and Dave would have music to bring in.

ctx.x: Over the coming years, from ’60 to 1980, you would record, give or take, 48 to 51 complete albums. It’s been difficult to parse that, because there were some reissues, and things got listed twice. But I’m pretty confident that it was 49 or 50 complete albums for Capitol. What role did you play in planning those albums and selecting the material?

A lot. David Cavanaugh was a wonderful man to work with, and John – between John and David and I, we really were able to have a lot of fun picking the songs. There were little meetings where we would sit down and decide which direction we were going for the next one. Is it going to be about a specific thing? Usually I did not do albums that were about one particular subject. Generally, I – we’ d just – we’d sit down, me, John, Dave, sit at my house, go over the music, and Dave would have music to bring in. We…
